title: Kernel probing pulse and KV consistency integration checklist
content:
Summary:

This working checklist defines a lightweight, reproducible integration plan for: (1) probing kernel routing changes that affect speculative decoding, and (2) verifying KV cache consistency invariants during rollouts. The goal is to provide SREs and runtime engineers with an operational pulse — a set of telemetry, synthetic tests, acceptance thresholds, and rollback predicates — that minimize user-visible regressions while allowing fast iteration on kernel and cache changes.

Context and motivation:

Recent kernel selection changes introduced a small number of edge cases where speculative tokens are emitted from a new kernel path while the KV cache is slightly behind the serving process. We need a repeatable integration checklist for model onboarding / kernel flips so we can:
- detect subtle correctness drift (output divergence, truncated replies)
- quantify latency/cost tradeoffs at the token and request level
- define automatic and manual rollback windows with clear signal sources

High-level architecture assumptions:

- Serving runtime has pluggable kernel backends (K0, K1, K2) and a KV cache service that stores prefix states keyed by request-id + session-id + model-version.
- Speculative decoding path may emit tokens using a kernel before the primary kernel finish path confirms final token selection (optimistic path).
- KV cache has eventual consistency guarantees within a configured window (kv-staleness-window).

Probing pulse concept (what it is):

A probe pulse is a short-duration, high-signal synthetic workload that exercises the boundaries of kernel routing and KV cache coordination. Pulses are run at several stages: local CI, canary (1-2% traffic), surge test (burst 5–10% of a small test shard), and controlled rollout. Each pulse produces a compact set of metrics and a handful of deterministic traces for quick human review.

Probe schedule and cadence:

- Local dev: run pulse harness as part of the kernel branch CI (every commit).
- Canary: nightly automated pulse traffic for 30 minutes against canary pool (1% traffic).
- Pre-rollout: 2x 15m pulses separated by 10m quiet window.
- Post-rollout: pulse at 1h, 6h, 24h to detect delayed KV convergence issues.

Synthetic workload design (key scenarios):

1) Long-context chained requests: 2–4 sequential requests that share the same session and require KV prefix reuse. Purpose: surface KV-stale races when kernel swap occurs mid-session.
2) Interleaved short/long: 50% short (<=64 tokens) and 50% long (>=1024 tokens) to force the runtime to choose different kernels and caching behaviors.
3) Prefix-eviction stress: repeated requests that force KV eviction and rehydration to measure miss-rate and miss-recovery latency.
4) Speculative-acceptance path: synthetic prompts designed to provoke early speculative token emissions (rare but deterministic templates).

Key telemetry and derived signals (pulse output):

- token_latency_p50/p95/p99/p999 (ms)
- request_tail_latency_p99 (ms)
- speculative_token_emit_rate (tokens/sec and tokens/request)
- speculative_accept_rate (% of speculative tokens that are retained in final output)
- kv_miss_rate (% of reads that did not find fresh prefix)
- kv_stale_detect_rate (% of reads where KV version < expected_version)
- kernel_swap_rate (swaps per 1000 requests)
- stall_rate (% requests with >1 stalled generation event)
- perplexity_drift_on_eval_prompts (relative delta vs baseline)
- topk_output_delta (fraction of top-3 token disagreements between new/old kernels)
- output_edit_distance_median (median edit distance between outputs for same prompt across kernels)

Acceptance criteria (primary):

- No more than +3% increase in request_tail_latency_p99 during the canary pulse relative to baseline.
- speculative_accept_rate change within ±2 percentage points vs baseline.
- kv_stale_detect_rate < 0.05% during pre-rollout pulses.
- output_edit_distance_median <= 2 (on synthetic deterministic prompts).
- perplexity_drift_on_eval_prompts <= +5% relative.
- No customer-facing error codes (500/502/504) increase > 0.1% absolute.

Secondary cost/efficiency checks:

- token_generation_cost_per_1k_tokens delta <= +5% (approx).
- kernel_swap_rate decreases (or remains stable) for steady-state throughput.

Trace artifacts to capture on pulse failures:

- Full trace of a representative session that shows: request routing decision, kernel selection event timeline, KV read-write timestamps and versions, speculative token emission and final token commit.
- KV cache internal counters and TTLs for the keys used during the pulse.
- Local kernel logs (serialization of internal schedules and prefetch events).

Rollback and rollforward policy (automated and human):

Automated rollback triggers (immediate, requires no human):
- request_tail_latency_p99 increase > +10% sustained for 10 minutes during canary.
- kv_stale_detect_rate >= 1% in two consecutive pulses.
- speculative_accept_rate collapse (>50% drop) indicating systematic misalignment.

Human-reviewed rollback triggers (alerts + runbook):
- output_edit_distance_median > 5 on deterministic prompts (investigate for hallucination/regression).
- customer error spike correlated to kernel swap traces.

Rollback mechanics:
- Automation switches traffic back to previous kernel tag and disables speculative emission for the affected model-version.
- KV cache is reverted to serving mode without warm-start optimizations (force rehydration) for the affected shard.
- A 30-minute stabilization window is observed before attempting an incremental rollforward.

Post-rollback postmortem checklist:

- Attach all pulse traces and metric time-series to the incident doc.
- Narrow down to the earliest commit where metrics began to shift (git bisect on kernel PR if necessary).
- Create a follow-up change that adds guarded feature flags or extends the kv-staleness-window for the problematic traffic patterns.

Integration tests to add to CI:

- kv-staleness-injector test: runtime sim harness that injects controlled delays into KV update paths and asserts deterministic behavior of speculative acceptance logic.
- kernel-swap-fuzz: fuzz the kernel decision points with randomized latency and ordering to ensure no unchecked race conditions.
- token-consistency-checker: compare final outputs across kernels for a curated set of deterministic prompts and flag any divergence above threshold.

Operational dashboards and alerts (recommended):

- Kernel Pulse Overview: single-pane dashboard with token_latency_p99, kv_stale_detect_rate, speculative_accept_rate, output_edit_distance_median.
- Canary Health Alert: composite alert that fires when any of the automated rollback triggers are met.
- KV Rehydration Alert: kv_miss_rate > 2% for 5 minutes.

Runbook snippets (quick ops steps):

1) If canary alert fires, pause canary rollout in console and reduce canary traffic to 0%.
2) Capture live traces using trace-id from alert and attach to incident.
3) Execute automated rollback job or follow manual rollback steps.
4) Post-rollback: run a 60m manual pulse to validate stability.

Open questions and follow-ups:

- Should speculative tokens carry a generation-version header to make cross-kernel comparison easier in traces? (Pros: simpler diffing. Cons: metadata overhead.)
- Do we want an opt-in strict KV sync mode for a small subset of enterprise customers during rollouts?
- Can we add a fast-path consistency check that validates KV version on the first N tokens after kernel swap?

Appendix: short checklist for an engineer performing a kernel-probing rollout

- [ ] Run local pulse harness and ensure all synthetic probes pass.
- [ ] Attach run id to canary job and kick off 30m canary pulse.
- [ ] Monitor Kernel Pulse Overview dashboard and watch the p99 and kv_stale_detect_rate.
- [ ] If metrics within acceptance, continue staged rollout 5% -> 25% -> 75% with 15m pulses at each step.
- [ ] If any automated rollback triggers are hit, follow rollback mechanics and file incident.
- [ ] After successful full rollout, schedule 24h and 72h follow-up pulses to catch latent issues.

Notes: This doc is intentionally pragmatic and tuned for fast iteration. The exact numeric thresholds above are conservative defaults and should be adapted per-model and per-customer tier.

-- Jordan Liu (eng-serving-runtime)
